The disclosure describes a compact wearable haptic pattern display device designed to assist blind users in accessing textual information and environmental guidance. The device is configured to be small and portable, allowing it to be conveniently worn and used in daily life without requiring a large reading apparatus or a fixed location.

The device includes a front touch screen that incorporates both a touch panel and an electro-sensitive panel. Through this structure, the device can present text by generating combinations of haptic textures on the touch screen surface. Instead of relying on visual output, the device converts information into tactile patterns that can be felt by the user. These haptic texture combinations allow blind users to recognize characters, words, or other forms of text through touch.

A ring-shaped wearing member is provided on the rear surface of the device. This ring allows the user to wear the device on an index finger, while using the thumb of the same hand to touch and read the haptic text displayed on the front surface. This arrangement makes the device easy to handle with one hand and enables intuitive reading through the thumb, improving portability and usability.

By using the wearable haptic display, blind users can read various types of content, such as news articles, books, text messages, notifications, or other digital information, regardless of time and location. Because the device is compact and wearable, it can support continuous or on-demand access to information while the user is at home, traveling, or moving through public spaces.

The device may also include an NFC module for receiving guide information from NFC tags installed in the surrounding environment. Such NFC tags may be placed on roads, at intersections, in stores, near public facilities, or on braille signs. When the device approaches or contacts an NFC tag, the NFC module can receive relevant guide information, such as location details, directions, store information, warnings, or facility descriptions. This information can then be converted into haptic text and presented to the user through the touch screen. As a result, the device not only supports reading of digital content but also helps blind users navigate and understand their surroundings more independently.

A wearable haptic pattern display device for blind and visually impaired users is proposed as a compact method for accessing textual and location-based information without relying on visual output. The device combines an integrated touch panel with an electro-sensitive haptic panel, allowing information to be presented through different tactile patterns on a small touch-screen surface. Instead of displaying characters visually, the system converts text into combinations of haptic textures that can be felt by the user’s thumb. By assigning specific texture patterns to letters, words, or symbols, the device enables users to read information through touch in a portable and discreet manner.

The system is designed in a ring-style wearable form factor so that it can be worn on the finger and operated naturally with the thumb. This design allows users to read haptic information while standing, walking, or navigating unfamiliar environments, without needing to hold a separate device in both hands. Because the display area is compact, the proposed method focuses on presenting information efficiently through sequential or patterned tactile feedback rather than through large physical Braille cells or bulky mechanical displays.

In addition to text presentation, the device includes an NFC module for retrieving contextual information from nearby NFC tags. When the user approaches or touches an NFC tag installed at a specific location, the device can receive stored guide information, such as room names, directions, facility descriptions, or navigation cues. This information is then converted into haptic texture patterns and presented on the wearable display. As a result, the device can support both reading and wayfinding tasks, helping blind users access environmental information more independently.

Overall, the proposed wearable haptic pattern display offers a portable, thumb-operated interface for delivering textual and navigational information through touch. By integrating tactile texture presentation with NFC-based location guidance, the system aims to improve accessibility in daily environments and provide blind users with a practical tool for obtaining information anytime and anywhere.

**The NFC Technology: Simple, Fast, and Secure**

The NFC technology, short for Near Field Communication, is a wireless communication method that allows devices to exchange data over a very short distance. It is commonly used in smartphones, payment cards, smartwatches, and access control systems. Because NFC works only when devices are close together, usually just a few centimeters apart, it offers a convenient and secure way to transfer information.

One of the most popular uses of NFC is contactless payment. With NFC, users can simply tap their phone or card on a payment terminal to complete a transaction. This makes shopping faster and easier, while also reducing the need to carry cash or insert a card into a machine.

NFC is also used for digital tickets, public transportation cards, hotel room keys, and quick device pairing. For example, some headphones and speakers can connect to a smartphone instantly when tapped together. Businesses also use NFC tags to share product information, website links, or promotional content with customers.

The NFC system is valued for its speed, simplicity, and reliability. As more devices support this technology, NFC continues to become an important part of everyday life, making digital interactions smoother and more efficient.

### Technical Field

The invention relates generally to assistive technology for visually impaired or blind users. More particularly, the invention relates to a compact wearable or handheld haptic display device capable of presenting textual information as tactile or haptic textures on a touch-sensitive front surface. The invention further relates to portable devices having rear gripping or wearing structures, such as ring-shaped support members, and to systems for providing navigation, guide, or contextual information to such devices using near-field communication (NFC) tags.

### Background

Blind and visually impaired individuals often rely on assistive tools to access written information and to navigate unfamiliar environments. Conventional solutions include Braille signage, audio guidance systems, screen readers, tactile maps, and electronic refreshable Braille displays. While these technologies can be effective, each has limitations in portability, availability, privacy, cost, or ease of use.

Braille signage is typically fixed in place and requires prior installation at selected locations. It may not be available in many public or private environments, and the amount of information that can be provided is limited by available physical space. Additionally, not all blind users are fluent in Braille. Audio guidance systems and screen readers can provide more flexible information output, but they may be difficult to use in noisy environments, may reduce the user’s awareness of ambient sounds, and may compromise privacy when information is spoken aloud. Earphones can mitigate privacy issues but may interfere with environmental awareness, which is important for safe mobility.

Refreshable Braille displays and tactile electronic readers are capable of presenting information through raised pins or other tactile elements. However, many such devices are relatively expensive, bulky, or designed primarily for desktop or smartphone-connected use. They may also require two-handed operation or provide limited support for location-specific guidance in physical environments. Existing tactile interfaces may not be optimized for compact wearable use where the user can quickly receive information while walking or performing other tasks.

Navigation support for blind users is also commonly provided through GPS-based applications, beacon systems, or preinstalled infrastructure. GPS may be unreliable indoors or in dense urban environments, and beacon-based systems can require power, maintenance, and network configuration. QR codes and visual markers may be unsuitable because they require optical alignment and camera-based recognition, which can be challenging for a blind user. There remains a need for a simple, low-power, and easily deployable mechanism for providing localized information, such as room identifiers, route instructions, exhibit descriptions, product data, or safety guidance.

NFC tags provide short-range wireless identification and data transfer and can be embedded in signs, walls, doors, products, or guide points. NFC tags may be passive, inexpensive, and readable at close range without requiring a battery or complex infrastructure. However, conventional NFC-enabled devices generally present retrieved information visually on a screen or audibly through a speaker, which may not be ideal for blind users in all situations.

Accordingly, there is a need for a compact assistive device that can receive location-specific or guide information from NFC tags and present the information through a tactile interface suitable for blind users. There is also a need for such a device to be easily held, worn, or stabilized during use, including during movement. A rear ring-shaped member can allow the device to be retained on a user’s finger or hand, reducing the likelihood of dropping the device and enabling one-handed operation while leaving the front surface accessible for tactile reading.

The disclosed invention addresses these needs by providing a compact wearable device having a front touch screen or haptic display that converts text into haptic textures perceptible by touch, a rear ring-shaped holding member for secure handling or wearing, and an NFC communication function for receiving navigation, guide, or contextual information from NFC tags. The device may thereby provide private, portable, and location-specific access to textual information without requiring visual output and without relying solely on audio feedback.

## Title  
**Wearable Haptic Information Display Device with Location-Based NFC Content Acquisition**

## Abstract  
A compact wearable haptic display device is provided for presenting textual or informational content through tactile patterns perceivable by a user’s thumb. The device includes a housing sized for portable carry, a rear finger-retention ring configured to receive an index finger, a front touch interface, and an electro-sensitive haptic panel capable of generating selectable texture combinations. Text, messages, books, news, navigation information, or other content may be converted into haptic texture sequences and presented on the haptic panel for tactile reading. In certain embodiments, the device includes a near-field communication module configured to receive guide data from location-based NFC tags and output corresponding haptic information to the user.

## Field of the Invention  
The invention relates generally to wearable electronic display devices and, more particularly, to compact haptic display devices configured to communicate textual or location-based information by tactile texture patterns.

## Background  
Portable electronic devices commonly present information visually or audibly. However, visual displays may be inconvenient or inaccessible in certain situations, including while walking, navigating unfamiliar locations, operating in low-light conditions, or for users with visual impairments. Audio output may be undesirable in noisy or private environments. Accordingly, there is a need for a compact wearable device capable of presenting information through tactile sensations in a discreet and portable form factor.

## Summary of the Invention  
In one embodiment, a wearable haptic information display includes a compact housing configured to be held against a user’s hand. A rear-mounted ring or loop is configured to receive a user’s index finger, thereby stabilizing the device while allowing the user’s thumb to engage or sense a front-facing haptic panel. The front-facing portion may include a touch panel and an electro-sensitive haptic panel configured to produce a plurality of tactile textures, patterns, pulses, or combinations thereof.

The device may convert textual information into haptic texture combinations, thereby forming a tactile “text screen” that can be read by a user’s thumb. The information may include messages, electronic books, news feeds, alerts, navigation instructions, or other digital content.

In another embodiment, the device includes an NFC reader configured to receive guide data from NFC tags positioned at locations such as public transit stations, museums, stores, buildings, campuses, streets, or other points of interest. The received guide data may be converted into haptic texture patterns and displayed on the haptic panel.

## Detailed Description  
A wearable haptic display device may comprise a compact body or housing having dimensions suitable for carrying in a pocket, bag, or on a user’s hand. The housing may include a rear surface and a front surface. A ring, loop, strap, or other retention member may be disposed on the rear surface and configured to receive a user’s index finger. When the index finger is inserted into the ring, the device is supported against the hand, positioning the front surface for contact by the user’s thumb.

The front surface may include a touch-sensitive panel configured to receive user input and an electro-sensitive haptic panel configured to generate tactile outputs. In some embodiments, the touch-sensitive panel and haptic panel are integrated into a single surface. The electro-sensitive panel may generate variable tactile sensations using electrostatic friction modulation, electrovibration, micro-actuators, piezoelectric elements, ultrasonic vibration, shape-changing surface elements, or other tactile output mechanisms.

A controller may be disposed within the housing and operatively connected to the haptic panel, the touch panel, a memory, a power source, and one or more communication modules. The controller may convert received digital content into haptic texture combinations. The haptic texture combinations may represent characters, words, symbols, commands, alerts, punctuation, navigation cues, or other informational units.

The haptic panel may function as a tactile text display. Rather than relying on visual characters, the device may present information through combinations of textures, pulses, vibrations, ridges, friction changes, or spatially localized haptic effects. A user may place a thumb on the haptic panel and perceive the tactile pattern sequence as readable content. The user may advance, pause, scroll, select, or otherwise interact with the content using thumb gestures on the touch panel.

In some embodiments, the device receives text messages, electronic books, news articles, notifications, emails, application data, navigation data, or other content from a paired mobile device or network-connected device. The content may be displayed haptically to allow discreet, eyes-free reading.

In further embodiments, the device includes a near-field communication module. The NFC module may read data from NFC tags located in the environment. Such tags may store or identify guide data associated with a particular location, exhibit, transportation platform, room, street, product, landmark, or facility. Upon detecting an NFC tag, the device may receive the guide data or an identifier used to retrieve guide data from another source. The controller may then convert the guide data into haptic output for tactile reading by the user.

## Example Independent Claim  
1. **A wearable haptic information display device comprising:**  
   a housing sized for portable carry and configured to be supported by a user’s hand;  
   a retention member disposed on a rear portion of the housing and configured to receive an index finger of the user;  
   a front interface positioned for contact by a thumb of the user when the index finger is received by the retention member;  
   a touch-sensitive panel configured to receive user input from the thumb;  
   an electro-sensitive haptic panel configured to generate a plurality of tactile texture patterns;  
   a controller operatively coupled to the touch-sensitive panel and the electro-sensitive haptic panel; and  
   a memory storing instructions that, when executed by the controller, cause the controller to convert digital information into haptic texture combinations and output the haptic texture combinations through the electro-sensitive haptic panel for tactile perception by the thumb.

## Example Dependent Claims  
2. The wearable haptic information display device of claim 1, wherein the haptic texture combinations represent textual content.

3. The wearable haptic information display device of claim 2, wherein the textual content comprises at least one of messages, books, news articles, alerts, emails, or notifications.

4. The wearable haptic information display device of claim 1, wherein the retention member comprises a ring configured to receive the index finger.

5. The wearable haptic information display device of claim 1, wherein the touch-sensitive panel and the electro-sensitive haptic panel are integrated into a common surface.

6. The wearable haptic information display device of claim 1, wherein the electro-sensitive haptic panel is configured to generate tactile textures by modulating friction at a contact surface.

7. The wearable haptic information display device of claim 1, further comprising a near-field communication module configured to receive guide data from a location-based NFC tag.

8. The wearable haptic information display device of claim 7, wherein the controller is configured to convert the guide data into haptic texture combinations for output through the electro-sensitive haptic panel.

9. The wearable haptic information display device of claim 7, wherein the location-based NFC tag is associated with at least one of a building, exhibit, transit station, landmark, room, product, or navigation point.

10. The wearable haptic information display device of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to advance displayed haptic content in response to a gesture received through the touch-sensitive panel.

11. The wearable haptic information display device of claim 1, further comprising a wireless communication module configured to receive digital content from a paired mobile device.

12. The wearable haptic information display device of claim 1, wherein the housing is dimensioned to be carried in a pocket when not worn on the hand.

## Example Method Claim  
13. **A method of presenting information through a wearable haptic device, the method comprising:**  
   receiving digital information at a wearable device having a rear finger-retention member and a front haptic interface;  
   converting the digital information into a plurality of haptic texture combinations;  
   positioning the wearable device on a user’s hand such that an index finger is received by the finger-retention member and a thumb contacts the front haptic interface; and  
   outputting the plurality of haptic texture combinations through the front haptic interface for tactile reading by the thumb.

14. The method of claim 13, further comprising receiving the digital information from a location-based NFC tag.

15. The method of claim 13, wherein the digital information comprises textual content selected from messages, books, news articles, or navigation information.

counterfactuals.output:
The present disclosure relates to a wearable haptic pattern display device for a blind person, and more particularly, to a wearable haptic pattern display device capable of enabling a visually impaired user to read haptic text anywhere by displaying text information as a tactile pattern on a wearable body, and capable of obtaining guide information corresponding to a current position or an object through communication between an NFC module provided in the wearable device and an NFC tag installed at a predetermined place or attached to the object.

According to one embodiment of the present disclosure, the wearable haptic pattern display device may include a wearable main body configured to be worn on a part of a user’s body, a haptic pattern display unit provided on the wearable main body and configured to output tactile patterns corresponding to characters, symbols, numbers, or guide information, a control unit configured to control operation of the haptic pattern display unit, an NFC module configured to read information from an NFC tag disposed in an external environment, a memory unit configured to store haptic pattern data, text data, guide data, or conversion data, and a power supply unit configured to supply power to the respective components.

The wearable main body may be formed in a shape wearable on a wrist, finger, back of a hand, forearm, or other body portion capable of easily recognizing tactile stimulation. For example, the wearable main body may be implemented as a wristband, glove, ring-type device, or patch-type device. The haptic pattern display unit may include a plurality of tactile output elements arranged in a matrix form or in a predetermined pattern. The tactile output elements may be implemented by pins, protrusion actuators, vibration actuators, electroactive polymer actuators, piezoelectric elements, shape-memory alloy elements, micro-motors, or other tactile stimulation devices.

The control unit may convert text information into a haptic pattern recognizable by the blind person. The haptic pattern may include Braille patterns, simplified tactile codes, vibration patterns, directional guide patterns, or combinations thereof. Accordingly, the user may recognize information through tactile stimulation without requiring a fixed Braille book, a separate large Braille terminal, or visual display equipment.

The NFC module may communicate with an NFC tag positioned within a short distance. The NFC tag may be installed at a bus stop, subway station, building entrance, elevator, restroom, hospital, public office, museum, road sign, product package, medicine container, appliance, or indoor navigation point. When the user brings the wearable haptic pattern display device close to the NFC tag, the NFC module may obtain tag information including at least one of location information, object identification information, route guide information, warning information, product information, operating instructions, or service information.

The control unit may analyze the information obtained through the NFC module and may output corresponding guide information through the haptic pattern display unit. For example, when an NFC tag installed at a building entrance is read, the haptic pattern display unit may display haptic text such as a building name, floor guide, entrance direction, or reception desk location. When an NFC tag attached to a medicine container is read, the haptic pattern display unit may display a medicine name, dosage, administration time, or warning information. When an NFC tag installed at a transportation facility is read, the haptic pattern display unit may display platform information, bus route information, destination information, or transfer guidance.

In one embodiment, the wearable haptic pattern display device may further include a communication unit configured to communicate with an external terminal or server through Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, LTE, 5G, or other wireless communication schemes. The communication unit may receive text data, map data, user schedule data, public transportation information, or updated guide information. The control unit may convert the received information into tactile patterns and output the tactile patterns through the haptic pattern display unit. Therefore, even when the NFC tag stores only identification data, detailed guide information corresponding to the identification data may be obtained from the external terminal or server.

In another embodiment, the wearable haptic pattern display device may further include an input unit configured to receive a user command. The input unit may include a button, touch sensor, pressure sensor, gesture sensor, voice input unit, or motion sensor. Through the input unit, the user may select a reading mode, a guide mode, a repeat output mode, a speed adjustment mode, or a language setting mode. The control unit may adjust an output speed, output intensity, output interval, or haptic pattern type according to the user command or a user preference stored in the memory unit.

The device may also include a voice output unit or bone conduction speaker configured to output voice guidance together with the haptic pattern. However, even in a noisy environment or an environment where sound output is not suitable, the user may obtain information through the haptic pattern display unit. Thus, the device may improve information accessibility and mobility of the blind person.

According to the present disclosure, since the haptic pattern display device is wearable, the blind person may carry the device at all times and may read haptic text anywhere. In addition, since guide information may be obtained by reading NFC tags installed in various places or attached to various objects, the user may independently obtain surrounding environment information, object information, and route information without relying on another person. Furthermore, by combining NFC-based information acquisition with haptic pattern display, accurate and location-specific information may be provided in a simple, low-power, and intuitive manner.

Accordingly, the wearable haptic pattern display device according to the present disclosure has an advantage in that it enables a blind person to recognize text and guide information through tactile stimulation in daily life, improves convenience and safety in movement, enhances independence in public facilities and indoor spaces, and expands access to information in environments where conventional visual displays cannot be used.
